nameStory: This bee gets its "thistle" name from its special fondness for visiting thistle flowers, where it's most commonly spotted by naturalists. The "longhorn" part refers to the impressively long antennae of the males, which can be nearly as long as their entire body. "Eastern" distinguishes it from similar western relatives that also love thistles but live across the continent.
description: The Eastern Thistle Longhorn Bee is a medium-sized native bee about the size of a small honeybee, with a fuzzy, robust body typically golden-brown to grayish in color. Like other longhorn bees, the males sport dramatically long, thread-like antennae that immediately catch your eye. These are solitary bees, meaning each female works alone to build her own nest rather than living in a hive. You'll spot them actively buzzing around flowers during the warmest months of summer.

idTips.label: Male antennae
idTips.description: Males have extraordinarily long, thin antennae that extend well beyond their head - almost like delicate black threads waving as they fly

idTips.label: Body fuzziness
idTips.description: Dense, soft hair covers the body, giving it a pleasantly fuzzy texture that's golden-brown to grayish, especially thick on the thorax

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: About honeybee-sized but more robust and stocky, with a noticeably rounder, less streamlined body shape

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Fast, purposeful flight between flowers with a slightly buzzy, droning sound as they work

idTips.label: Thistle preference
idTips.description: Frequently seen clinging to purple thistle flowers, often becoming dusted with white or purple pollen

habitat: Look for Eastern Thistle Longhorn Bees in sunny, open areas where thistles and other late-summer wildflowers bloom abundantly - old fields, meadows, roadsides, and prairie remnants. They prefer areas with sandy or well-drained soil where females can excavate their underground nests. You'll often find them in the same spots where Canada thistle, bull thistle, and asters create colorful late-summer displays.

seasonality.spring: Not active - still developing underground in their nest cells from the previous year's eggs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from mid-July through August, when you'll see both males and females actively foraging on flowers and males pursuing females for mating.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down in early September as adults complete their life cycle, though a few stragglers may visit late-blooming asters.
seasonality.winter: Completely inactive - next year's generation overwinters as larvae in underground nest cells.

funFact: Male Eastern Thistle Longhorn Bees often sleep communally, clustering together on plant stems overnight in what bee researchers call "sleeping aggregations" - imagine finding a dozen fuzzy bees lined up like tiny sleeping bags on a single flower stalk at dawn!
confusionNotes: The extremely long antennae on males make this group unmistakable, but telling apart different Melissodes species requires close examination of subtle features like hair color and body proportions. Remember: if it's a fuzzy bee on thistles with crazy-long antennae, you've found a male longhorn bee - the exact species takes more detective work!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "longhorn bees," these insects are completely unrelated to longhorn beetles or cattle - the name simply describes their antenna length. Many people assume all bees live in hives, but longhorn bees are solitary, with each female digging her own burrow and stocking it with pollen balls for her offspring.
compareHints: Eastern Thistle Longhorn Bees are best distinguished from their Melissodes cousins by their timing and flower preferences - they're active later in summer than most relatives and show a strong preference for thistle flowers. The Common Longhorn Bee is active earlier and visits a broader range of flowers, while the Two-spotted Longhorn Bee has distinctive pale markings on the face that this species typically lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the nine other Melissodes species in New England, the Two-spotted Longhorn Bee is distinguished primarily by those diagnostic pale spots.
Among its Melissodes relatives, Drury's Long-horned Bee is distinguished by its rustic brown coloration and preference for a wide variety of late-season flowers.

Among its Melissodes relatives, the Dark-veined Longhorn Bee stands out for having the most conspicuous dark wing veins - while Common Longhorn Bees and Two-spotted Longhorn Bees have similar body shapes and fuzzy appearance, their wing veins are typically lighter and less noticeable.
Among its longhorn bee relatives, the Denticulate Longhorn Bee is most reliably distinguished by its strong association with ironweed flowers rather than physical features alone.
